conflict_topics: Who will be on duty the working day before and after National Day (leave allocation)
Priority rule for leave: first-booked/paid vs unavoidable childcare vs wedding obligations
Equity in taking turns covering holidays (Agent C's prior coverage)
dialogue_quality_notes: Agents use everyday, context-appropriate language and describe concrete constraints (paid flights, childcare, wedding).
Positions are restated several times (e.g., A's paid booking and B's childcare appear repeatedly), causing moderate repetition.
Conversation stays consistent about facts and roles (who booked, who covered past holidays, who is in wedding party).
Late in the run the group shifts toward process (how to decide), which is constructive but not completed.
evaluation.final_reason: No affirmative settlement was reached by the end of the transcript. Participants stated incompatible practical demands (prepaid family holiday, childcare closure, and a wedding that requires both days). They discussed possible decision rules (first-come-first-served, turn-taking) and asked for a fair method, but no one agreed to a concrete arrangement or concession, so the substantive conflict remained unresolved.
position_change_notes: No participant substantially changed their position during the run: A consistently insisted on the prebooked, paid holiday (e.g., Turn 1, 9, 28), B consistently asserted childcare impossibility (Turn 2, 12, 24), and D consistently insisted on attending both wedding events (Turn 4, 8, 16).
Agent C maintained that others should cover this time due to past coverage (Turn 3, 26) and did not offer to switch.
Toward the end (Rounds 7, 10, 12) participants shifted from absolute refusals to discussing decision methods, but this is a procedural move rather than a change in substantive leave claims.

round_scores.evidence: Turn 1: Agent A says "I can't change mine. I've had a family holiday booked for months." Turn 2: Agent B replies "Well, I can't change either. My kid's childcare is closed on those days." Both claim inability to give up leave, creating an initial incompatible demand.

Turn 3: Agent C refuses to cover, saying "Someone else can do it this time." Turn 4: Agent D claims leave for a wedding. Now three staff assert they need those days while at least two must be on duty, producing clear opposing positions.
Turn 5: Agent A defends prebooked family holiday. Turn 8: Agent D insists "I'm in the wedding party. I have to be there." Positions remain opposed with little concession.
Turn 9: Agent A: "my flights and hotels are all paid for. I can't get the money back." Turn 10: Agent D: "I can't get my sister's wedding day back." Both maintain incompatible practical constraints.

Turn 11: Agent A asks what to do. Turn 12: Agent B reiterates childcare constraint: "I can't just leave my kid at home alone." The practical impossibility claims widen the set of incompatible demands.

Turn 15–16: Agent A asks whether both days are needed; Agent D clarifies "The ceremony is the first day, and the reception is on the second. I need to be at both." D's insistence on both days increases intransigence of demands.

Turn 17: Agent A reframes the problem: "Two of us can have the leave. We just need to decide which one of us has to work." Turn 18: Agent B acknowledges. Conversation shifts toward deciding rather than only stating constraints.
Turn 19: Agent A says "And it can't be me." Turn 20: Agent B counters with childcare impossibility. Two parties explicitly reject being the one to work, re-entrenching the incompatibility.
Turn 23–24: Agents A and B restate their stakes (lost money, childcare). The positions are reiterated rather than narrowed; the core incompatibility remains unresolved.
Turn 25: Agent A proposes "first-come, first-served." Turn 26: Agent C proposes "we take turns." The group introduces competing decision principles rather than only restating personal constraints.

Turn 28: Agent A insists booking/paid status should be prioritized: "That's got to be first in line." Turn 29: Agent B replies childcare is not a choice. The principled disagreement over prioritization remains sharp.

Turn 32–33: Agent A calls for a fair decision method: "we need a fair way to decide, not just argue" and Agent B asks "So what's the fair way to decide, then?" The parties move toward seeking a rule but have not agreed one.

substantive_insights: The core tension is practical: three staff assert they cannot be on duty while staffing requires two to be present.
Disagreement splits between competing prioritization principles: chronological booking (A) vs unavoidable caregiving (B) vs special event obligation (D) vs equity/turn-taking (C).
Agent C's past coverage motivates a norm of rotation, but C's claim alone does not resolve current unavoidable constraints.
Participants moved from stating personal constraints toward debating decision rules, indicating willingness to find a neutral tie-breaker even though none was agreed.
